question: Why are AC motors less troublesome than DC motors?

options.text: They run only at high altitude
They need no power supply at all once started
They need larger brushes than DC motors

explanation: DC motors suffer from commutation and arcing, worse at high altitude; AC motors avoid this.

question: How can brush problems stop a DC motor?

options.text: Brushes wear so fast that the motor speeds up
Hot brushes stick and lose contact
Brushes short the field to earth every revolution

explanation: Heat makes the brushes stick in their holders; contact resistance rises, sometimes to an open circuit, and the motor stops.

question: Do synchronous AC motors use brush gear?

options.text: Yes, for the rotor's low DC
Yes, for the full load current
Yes, for the AC to the stator windings

explanation: Synchronous motors feed their rotors with relatively low DC through slip rings, which is far less troublesome than commutation.

question: Why are AC motors suited to constant-speed applications?

options.text: Their speed is set by frequency
Their speed is set by the load only
Their speed is set by the supply voltage

explanation: An AC motor's speed is determined by the frequency of the supply, so a constant frequency gives a constant speed.

question: What makes the rotor of an AC motor turn?

options.text: A permanent magnet in the stator
A DC supply to the stator
A commutator reversing the rotor current

explanation: AC applied to the stator produces a rotating magnetic field, which drags the rotor round.

question: What are the two main types of AC motor used in aircraft?
explanation: Synchronous motors have a DC-fed rotor; induction motors have an unpowered rotor in which current is induced.

question: In a synchronous motor, how are the stator and rotor supplied?

options.text: DC to the stator, AC to the rotor
AC to the stator, DC to the rotor

explanation: A synchronous motor is basically an alternator run as a motor: AC on the stator, DC on the rotor.

question: In an induction motor, how is the rotor supplied?
explanation: The induction motor's rotor has no supply; its current is induced by the stator's rotating field.

question: Why is the synchronous motor so named?

options.text: It runs from a synchronising bus
Its rotor keeps step with the field
It needs a synchroniser to start
It must be paralleled with an alternator

explanation: The rotor, magnetised by DC, locks onto the rotating field and turns at exactly the same speed.

question: What is the construction of a synchronous motor basically the same as?
explanation: It is built like a rotating field alternator, with a DC-fed rotor inside a three-phase stator.

question: What happens to the speed of a synchronous motor as its load changes?

options.text: It varies with the supply voltage
It rises as the load rises
It falls as the load rises

explanation: Synchronous motors are single-speed motors: speed depends on supply frequency, not load.

question: A 4-pole synchronous motor runs on 400 Hz. At what speed does it turn?
explanation: RPM = f × 60 ÷ (poles ÷ 2) = 400 × 60 ÷ 2 = 12 000 RPM. Using 4 instead of 2 gives 6000.

question: An 8-pole synchronous motor runs on 400 Hz. At what speed does it turn?
A synchronous motor has the same number of poles as the alternator supplying it. Its speed is:
explanation: With equal pole numbers, the motor turns at the same speed as the alternator driving its supply.

question: What is a disadvantage of the synchronous motor?

options.text: It cannot run on three phase

explanation: It must be brought near synchronous speed before it locks in; induction windings are added to the rotor to start it.

question: How is a synchronous motor brought up to speed?

options.text: An external DC motor in every case

explanation: Extra induction windings on the rotor let it start like an induction motor until it nears synchronous speed.

question: What drives the synchronous motor of an engine RPM indicator?
explanation: A tacho-generator driven by the engine produces a supply whose frequency is proportional to engine speed.

question: Why does a tacho-generator system show engine RPM?

options.text: Its phase sequence changes with speed
Its voltage is fixed at all speeds
Its current is set by the battery

explanation: The generator frequency follows engine RPM, so the synchronous motor in the indicator turns at a speed proportional to engine RPM.

question: How is the indicator needle driven in a synchronous-motor RPM indicator?

options.text: Directly geared to the motor shaft
Through a magnet and drag cup
By a hairspring and moving coil

explanation: The motor spins a magnet that drags a drag cup round against a spring; the faster the motor, the further the needle moves.

question: Why is the induction motor so named?

options.text: It induces voltage in the stator
It needs an inductor to start
It is fed from an induction coil
Current is induced in its rotor

explanation: The rotating stator field induces alternating current in the rotor.

question: Why is the induction motor the most commonly used AC motor?

options.text: It needs a DC rotor supply
It runs at exactly synchronous speed
It is simple, robust and cheap
It has the most complex rotor

explanation: It is simple and robust, and cheap because its rotor is self-contained and not connected to the supply.

question: What is a squirrel cage rotor?

options.text: Copper bars joined by end rings
A wound rotor fed through slip rings

explanation: Longitudinal copper bars set in a laminated iron core, joined at each end by rings of the same material.

question: Why are the rotor bars of a squirrel cage of very low resistance?

options.text: So that no current can flow in them
So that a large current can flow in them
So that the rotor stays cool without any current
So that the rotor can be fed with DC

explanation: Low resistance lets a large induced current flow, producing a strong rotor field and torque.

question: How does an induction motor produce torque?

options.text: The rotor is fed with DC like a magnet
The stator field stays still while the rotor moves
The commutator reverses the rotor current

explanation: The rotating field cuts the rotor bars, inducing a large current whose own field interacts with the stator field to produce torque.

question: What decides the number of stator windings of an induction motor?

options.text: The size of the rotor bars

explanation: The stator windings are related to the number of poles and the number of phases of the supply.

question: How can a three-phase induction motor be reversed?
explanation: Reversing two phases reverses the direction of the rotating field and so of the motor.

question: Why can an induction motor's rotor never reach synchronous speed?

options.text: No flux would cut the rotor bars

explanation: At synchronous speed the rotor would move with the field, nothing would cut the bars and no torque would be produced.

question: What is slip speed?

options.text: The rotor speed divided by the frequency
The rotor speed at no load
The speed at which the motor stalls

explanation: Slip (rotor slip) is the difference between the speed of the rotating field and the rotor.

question: What is a typical slip for an induction motor?
explanation: A typical slip is around 5%.

question: Why is an induction motor sometimes called asynchronous?

options.text: It is not connected to a synchronising bus
It runs from a DC supply
Its rotor turns slower than the stator field
Its rotor turns faster than the stator field

explanation: Because of slip the rotor never quite keeps step with the field, so the motor is asynchronous.

question: What decides the speed of an induction motor?

options.text: The number of rotor bars fitted only

explanation: Speed is set by frequency, and slip increases slightly with load.

question: A 4-pole induction motor runs on 400 Hz with 5% slip. Roughly how fast does it turn?
explanation: Synchronous speed is 12 000 RPM; 5% slip gives 12 000 × 0.95 = 11 400 RPM. The rotor turns slower, never faster, than synchronous speed.

question: Is a single-phase induction motor self-starting?
explanation: A single-phase supply produces a pulsating, not rotating, field, so the motor needs help to start.

question: What is the most common way of starting a single-phase induction motor?

options.text: A DC supply to the rotor

explanation: A split phase winding, with its current shifted from the main winding, creates a rotating field for starting.

question: How far should the split phase current be shifted from the main winding current?
explanation: A lead or lag of 90° between the split phase and main winding currents produces a rotating field.

question: Which method can produce the phase shift in a split phase winding?
explanation: The shift may be produced by resistance, inductance, resistance-inductance or capacitance starting.

question: Capacitance-started motors usually have an output of:
explanation: The method chosen depends on output; capacitance-started motors are usually below 2 horsepower.

question: One phase fails on a lightly loaded three-phase induction motor that is running. What is likely?

options.text: It stops at once and cannot run
It hums on but will not restart

explanation: A running motor may keep turning on two phases, humming; the fault often goes unnoticed in a remote location until it will not start next time.

question: Why might a phase failure on a three-phase motor go unnoticed?

options.text: The motor stops and lights a warning
The fuse always blows at once

explanation: Motors are usually in remote locations, so the humming of a motor running on two phases is not noticed until it fails to start.
